title: To End High School Tracking, We Need to End Tracking in Elementary School
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler uses Montgomery County's move to put all high school students in honors classes to argue that high school tracking cannot be fixed at high school. She sketches the history of tracking and says the persistent cause is that disadvantaged students arrive unprepared for high school work, not merely low expectations or bias. She locates the origin in elementary "leveled reading," where comprehension is treated as a skill and struggling readers are confined to easy texts and pulled away from content subjects. Because background knowledge is the main determinant of comprehension, she says, leveled reading widens knowledge gaps that later look like ability differences. Her remedy is a coherent, topic-focused curriculum that gives all children the knowledge advantaged children pick up at home.
points: Renaming standard classes honors is likely to push high achievers into AP and IB, leaving honors as the new standard track.
Differences in academic preparation visible in high school begin earlier, so reforms aimed only at high school are doomed.
Leveled reading is openly embraced tracking in elementary school and has no evidence behind it.
Pulling struggling readers from science and social studies for skills instruction denies them the knowledge that drives comprehension.
Knowledge-rich elementary curricula that stay on a topic for weeks are the proposed fix.
quotes: The reason for the persistence of tracking isn’t just a matter of low teacher expectations. Nor is the fundamental cause racism or implicit bias. The basic problem is that—just as in the late 19th and early 20th century—many students, and especially those who are disadvantaged, are arriving at high school unprepared to do high school-level work.

If schools make honors classes the default setting, as those in Montgomery County are doing, what will likely happen is that higher-achieving students will desert them in favor of those college-level classes, turning honors classes into the de facto standard track.

There’s no evidence this system works, and for good reason. Cognitive scientists have known for decades that the most important determinant of reading comprehension isn’t abstract skill; it’s how much background knowledge the reader has relating to the topic.

Especially since the advent of high-stakes reading tests, the lower groups are also the least likely to get exposure to subjects that might actually build their knowledge, because the theory is that working on “reading” is more important. Struggling readers are often pulled out from social studies or science classes to receive extra “skills” instruction.
That leveling—or tracking, if you will—isn’t impossible to undo once students reach high school, but it requires a lot more than putting everyone in classes labeled “honors.

If you want to see tracking that is not only openly conducted but enthusiastically embraced—and that is the root cause of the de facto tracking that inevitably occurs in high school—all you have to do is look at American elementary schools.
